messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 68
- Gender: Male
- Ethnicity: North American
- Relationship Status: Married
- Occupation: School Counselor
- Trauma Type: Assault
- Pcl5: 62

He is 68 now, a school counselor who has spent most of his adult life listening carefully to children whose bodies tense before their words come. He is the kind of man who keeps peppermint in his desk drawer, remembers who has a court date coming up, and notices when a student’s silence means more than refusal. For decades he believes that calm attention can steady almost anything. That belief is what makes the night of the assault feel, to him, not only frightening but disorienting in a deeper way.

It happens a little over two years ago, on an early autumn evening. He stays late at the school after a parent meeting, finishing emails and straightening handouts for the next day. By the time he leaves, the parking lot is mostly empty. He remembers the cold air, the weight of his satchel, the automatic thought that he should have gone home sooner because his wife has made soup. He hears footsteps before he fully registers them. A man comes up fast behind him, grabs him hard, and demands his wallet. He tries, reflexively, to speak in the same measured voice he uses with agitated students—“Take it, just take it”—but the man strikes him anyway. He falls awkwardly against the pavement, feels a burst of pain in his ribs, and has a confused, vivid awareness of his cheek against the asphalt. He thinks, with a shocking clarity, I could die here in the school parking lot. The man kicks him once more, snatches the satchel, and runs.

For weeks afterward, he tells the story like a practical sequence of events: police, emergency room, bruising, a cracked rib, replacing cards and keys. He says he is lucky. His wife says the same, and he agrees because it is objectively true. But his body does not seem to understand that the danger is over. The first nights, he startles awake drenched in sweat, certain someone is standing in the bedroom doorway. He dreams not of the full attack but of fragments—the footsteps, the impact, the helpless position of being on the ground unable to see behind him. During the day he hears shoes scuffing in the hallway at school and feels his stomach drop before his mind catches up.

He goes back to work sooner than his wife thinks he should. At first he frames this as duty. Students need consistency, he says. But returning does not restore him. He begins arriving after sunrise even though he used to enjoy the quiet of the early building. He parks as close to the entrance as possible and scans the lot before stepping out of the car. If a parent conference runs late, he feels himself getting irritable, watching the windows darken. More than once, a custodian offers to walk him out, and he accepts with embarrassed gratitude. He hates that he now calculates exits in rooms he has sat in for years.

At home, his wife notices the shrinking of his world before he names it. He stops taking evening walks with her. He no longer wants to go to restaurants if parking means crossing a dark lot. When their daughter invites them to a school concert for their grandson, he agrees, then spends the entire event positioned near the aisle, unable to follow the music because he is tracking every person who enters. He keeps replaying the assault in ways that make no sense even to him: if he had left earlier, if he had handed over the bag faster, if he had shouted louder. He is a man who speaks gently to children about self-blame, yet he lies awake prosecuting himself with merciless logic.

The hardest part for him is what happens in the counseling office. A large eighth-grade boy, angry after being sent out of class, slams the door and raises his voice. Instantly, his pulse races. He feels heat in his face and a wild urge to get distance, to stand where he can see the boy’s hands. He manages the meeting, but afterward he closes his office door and sits very still, ashamed of how afraid he has felt. He begins doubting his instincts, the very instincts on which his career has rested. He wonders whether students can see the change in him: the moments when he flinches, the way his attention drifts when he hears commotion in the corridor, the fatigue around his eyes after another broken night of sleep.

His wife says he is here and not here. He knows what she means. He is more easily angered, then guilty for it. He forgets small things. He avoids the parking lot where it happened, taking a longer route to enter the school from the front. Some mornings he sits in his car gripping the steering wheel, gathering himself before he can walk inside. He still cares deeply about the children he counsels, especially the frightened ones, but now their stories sometimes open something raw in him. He recognizes in their vigilance a language his own body has begun to speak. And this unsettles him most of all: after a lifetime of helping others feel safe, he no longer experiences safety as something simple or durable, but as a fragile state that can vanish between one footstep and the next.
